question: How did you build this portfolio?
answer:
This portfolio (v2.0) is a next-generation rebuild of my original portfolio — built entirely with HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6 Modules). No frameworks, no backend, no AI API, completely offline.

question: Why did you choose Vanilla JavaScript for this portfolio?
answer:
A deliberate choice with a clear reason: to demonstrate deep JavaScript fundamentals.

Anyone can use React or Next.js to build a portfolio — but building the same result with Vanilla JavaScript proves that I understand the DOM, event delegation, module patterns, async data fetching, and state management at a fundamental level.

Specifically, this portfolio required:

  • A custom DataService singleton for async JSON loading and caching.
  • A custom terminal emulator with command parsing, history, and formatted output.
  • A tab management system with state tracking across the file explorer.
  • A modular component architecture — all in Vanilla JS without any framework.

It is the same reason I built ImgNinja entirely in Vanilla JS with Canvas API — because understanding the underlying platform makes me a better developer regardless of what framework I use next.

question: How does ECHO Bot work?
answer:
ECHO Bot is a predefined Q&A assistant built specifically for this portfolio. It is not a general-purpose AI chatbot.

How it works:

  • All questions and answers are stored in a JSON file: data/ai/echo-qa.json.
  • The DataService.js fetches this file on page load and makes the data available to the ECHO Bot component.
  • When you click a question, ECHO Bot looks up the corresponding answer from the JSON data and displays it with a typewriter animation.
  • There is no AI API, no backend, no network call after initial load — everything runs completely offline in the browser.

It was built this way to serve as an intelligent portfolio navigator rather than a general chatbot — guiding visitors to the right information quickly and professionally.

question: What is your problem-solving approach?
answer:
My problem-solving approach is structured and iterative:

  • Break it down: I decompose the problem into its smallest components rather than trying to tackle the whole thing at once.
  • Understand before fixing: I try to understand why the problem exists, not just apply a workaround. For example, when ImgNinja had memory issues with large files, I researched the full object URL lifecycle and canvas cleanup patterns rather than just limiting file size.
  • Research deeply: Official documentation, GitHub issues, and existing solutions all inform my approach. I never copy-paste without understanding.
  • Prototype and test: I write an isolated test case or proof-of-concept before integrating a solution. This is how I validated the binary search compression algorithm for ImgNinja before integrating it into the full tool.
  • Refactor: After a solution works, I clean up the code, add comments, and ensure it is maintainable.

question: How do you debug problems?
answer:
My debugging workflow depends on the type of problem:

  • Browser issues: Chrome DevTools is my primary tool — Network tab for API calls, Console for JS errors, Sources for step-through debugging, and Performance tab for bottlenecks.
  • Backend issues: Postman for API endpoint testing, console.log tracing, and environment variable verification.
  • Logic bugs: I isolate the problem into the smallest possible reproduction case, then work outward. For example, the binary search compression algorithm in ImgNinja was developed and tested in isolation before integration.
  • Cross-browser issues: I use feature detection and fallback patterns — learned from ImgNinja's challenge with Safari's WebP/AVIF support.
  • Tools I use: VS Code, Chrome DevTools, Postman, and XAMPP for local PHP development.

question: What is your development workflow?
answer:
My typical project workflow:

  • 6. Testing & Polish: Test edge cases, optimize for mobile, run Lighthouse audits, and clean up code before deployment.
  • 7. Deployment: Deploy to Vercel, GitHub Pages, or cPanel hosting depending on the project type.

question: How do you organize your projects?
answer:
My project organization follows the principle of separation of concerns — each layer of the application has a clear, dedicated location.

For a React/TypeScript project (like ScaleIQ): components/, pages/, hooks/, types/, styles/, constants/, data/, routes/, layouts/.

For a Vanilla JS project (like this portfolio): js/services/ for data fetching, js/components/ for UI logic, js/core/ for utilities, styles/ with base/layout/component categories, and data/ for all JSON data files.

For a PHP multi-page project (like RozgarSetu): shared includes/ for header/navbar/footer, dedicated PHP files per page, and a services/ subdirectory for service detail pages.

I use Git for version control on all projects.

question: What are the browser APIs you have worked with?
answer:
I have significant hands-on experience with the following browser APIs:

  • Canvas API: Used extensively in ImgNinja for image rendering, format-specific encoding (JPEG, WebP, PNG), pixel manipulation, and memory-efficient cleanup. Also used in the Retro Snake Game for 2D game rendering.
  • File API & FileReader API: For handling file uploads in ImgNinja — reading file contents, processing binary data, and drag-and-drop file selection.
  • Blob API & URL.createObjectURL: For generating downloadable output files in ImgNinja with proper object URL lifecycle management to prevent memory leaks.
  • LocalStorage API: Used in the Retro Snake Game for high score persistence and in other projects for client-side state.
  • Web Speech API: Used in BitBot for text-to-speech and speech-to-text voice input/output in the chatbot interface.
